subject: Polity
sub_topic: Chief Minister and State Council of Ministers

concepts.name: Appointment of Chief Minister: Constitutional Provisions and Conventions
key_dimensions: Article 164 — Governor appoints CM; no explicit qualification criteria beyond being a member of state legislature
Convention vs. discretion: Governor's role when no clear majority vs. post-election scenario
Appointment of a non-member as CM and the 6-month rule (must become member within 6 months)
UPSC trap: CM need not be a member of the Legislative Assembly — can be from Legislative Council if it exists

concepts.name: Tenure, Salary, and Security of the Chief Minister
key_dimensions: CM holds office 'during the pleasure of the Governor' (Article 164) — but this pleasure is not absolute
Real security: CM cannot be removed as long as majority is maintained in the Legislative Assembly
Salary and allowances charged to Consolidated Fund of the State (not votable)
UPSC trap: Contrast with President's fixed 5-year term — CM has no fixed tenure

concepts.name: Powers and Functions of the Chief Minister: Constitutional and Conventional
key_dimensions: Article 167: CM's duties — communicating decisions of Council of Ministers to Governor, furnishing information as required
Head of government vs. Governor as Head of State — real executive power vests in CM
CM's role in formation, expansion, and dismissal of Council of Ministers
CM as link between Governor and Council of Ministers — critical coordinating role

concepts.name: Composition and Size of State Council of Ministers
key_dimensions: 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003: Total ministers (including CM) not to exceed 15% of total strength of Legislative Assembly
Minimum floor: Not less than 12 ministers (important exception for small states)
Anti-defection linkage: A disqualified member cannot be appointed as minister
UPSC trap: 15% cap applies to Legislative Assembly strength, NOT both Houses combined

concepts.name: Categories of Ministers: Cabinet, Ministers of State, and Deputy Ministers
key_dimensions: Three-tier hierarchy: Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State (independent charge or attached), Deputy Ministers
Cabinet vs. Council of Ministers — critical distinction UPSC frequently tests
Cabinet has no mention in the Constitution; Council of Ministers is a constitutional body (Article 163, 164)
Parliamentary Secretaries: fourth category, sometimes appointed and their constitutional validity

concepts.name: Cabinet vs. Council of Ministers: Constitutional and Functional Distinction
key_dimensions: Council of Ministers is the constitutional body; Cabinet is a conventional, smaller body within it
Cabinet: senior ministers who meet regularly and take key policy decisions — not mentioned in Constitution
44th Amendment Act, 1978 inserted 'Cabinet' in Article 352 for the first time — only instance of constitutional mention
UPSC trap: Collective responsibility applies to entire Council of Ministers, not just the Cabinet

concepts.name: Collective Responsibility of Council of Ministers (Article 164)
key_dimensions: Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly of the State (Article 164(2))
Doctrine of collective responsibility: all ministers must publicly support Cabinet decisions or resign
Vote of no-confidence: applies to entire Council, not individual ministers — CM must resign with entire team
UPSC trap: Collective responsibility is to Legislative Assembly only, NOT the Legislative Council

concepts.name: Individual Responsibility of Ministers
key_dimensions: Ministers individually responsible to the CM — can be asked to resign or dismissed by Governor on CM's advice
Governor acts on CM's advice in removing a minister — limits discretionary power of Governor here
Contrast with collective responsibility: individual responsibility relates to minister's own portfolio and conduct
No constitutional provision explicitly mentions individual responsibility — it is a convention

concepts.name: Governor's Discretion vs. Aid and Advice of Council of Ministers (Article 163)
key_dimensions: Article 163: Governor acts on aid and advice of Council of Ministers EXCEPT in matters where he is required to act in his discretion
Governor's discretion is limited and judicially reviewable — Shamsher Singh vs. State of Punjab (1974)
Key discretionary powers: appointing CM when hung assembly, dismissing government that lost majority, referring bill for President's assent
UPSC trap: Governor cannot ask Council of Ministers to reconsider advice more than once (unlike President)

concepts.name: Relationship Between CM and Governor: Constitutional Provisions and Judicial Pronouncements
key_dimensions: Article 167 obligations: CM must communicate all decisions, furnish information, and submit for Governor's consideration any matter a minister has decided but Council has not considered
Sarkaria Commission recommendations on Governor-CM relationship and conventions
Punchhi Commission: Governor should not be a 'prolonged' obstacle — pocket veto issue
Recent controversies: Governors delaying assent to Bills — Punjab, Kerala, Tamil Nadu — SC rulings on deemed assent

concepts.name: Appointment, Oath, and Qualifications of State Ministers
key_dimensions: Ministers appointed by Governor on advice of CM (Article 164(1))
Qualification: Must be member of state legislature; if not, must become member within 6 months
Oath administered by Governor: oath of office AND oath of secrecy (Article 164(3))
UPSC trap: A person who is not a member of either House of state legislature CAN be appointed minister for up to 6 months

concepts.name: Council of Ministers and Confidence of Legislative Assembly: Vote of No-Confidence
key_dimensions: Council of Ministers holds office as long as it enjoys confidence of the Legislative Assembly
Floor test vs. trust vote — Governor can call for a floor test using discretionary power
Anti-defection law impact on stability of government — 10th Schedule linkage
UPSC trap: Legislative Council (Upper House) CANNOT move or pass a vote of no-confidence against the Council of Ministers

concepts.name: Role of CM in State Legislature: Legislative and Constitutional Functions
key_dimensions: CM advises Governor on summoning, proroguing, and dissolving the Legislative Assembly
CM's role in Governor's Address to the Legislature (Article 176) — policy content determined by Council of Ministers
CM's power to recommend dissolution of Assembly — Governor is not bound but convention exists
UPSC trap: Governor can refuse dissolution if CM has lost majority — Nabam Rebia case (2016) implications

concepts.name: CM's Role in Appointments to Key Constitutional and Statutory Bodies
key_dimensions: CM's advice in appointment of State Election Commission, State Public Service Commission (though formally by Governor)
CM's role in appointment of Advocate General (Article 165) — Governor appoints on CM's advice
Distinction: Some appointments Governor makes at discretion vs. on CM's advice
UPSC trap: Advocate General is appointed by Governor, NOT by the CM directly — but on CM's advice

concepts.name: Disqualification of Ministers and Anti-Defection Implications (91st Amendment)
key_dimensions: 91st Amendment Act, 2003: A member disqualified under the 10th Schedule cannot be appointed as a minister
This plugged the earlier loophole where defectors were rewarded with ministerial posts
Cap on ministers (15%) combined with anti-defection provisions creates a two-pronged accountability mechanism
UPSC trap: The 91st Amendment applies to both Union and State Councils of Ministers simultaneously

concepts.name: State Cabinet Committees: Role, Types, and Significance
key_dimensions: Cabinet Committees are extra-constitutional, conventional devices to manage workload
Types: Standing committees (permanent) and Ad hoc committees (temporary)
Can include non-Cabinet ministers; their decisions are binding as Cabinet decisions
UPSC trap: Cabinet committees are not mentioned in the Constitution — formed under business rules/conventions

concepts.name: Doctrine of Pleasure and Dismissal of Council of Ministers
key_dimensions: Governor's pleasure is not personal pleasure — it is conditional on majority in Legislative Assembly (B.R. Kapur vs. State of Tamil Nadu)
Governor cannot dismiss CM/Council if they enjoy majority — this distinguishes it from arbitrary dismissal
Difference from Union level: President's pleasure regarding PM is similarly conditioned by Lok Sabha majority
UPSC trap: Governor CAN dismiss a minister individually (on CM's advice) but cannot dismiss CM who has Assembly majority

concepts.name: CM and President's Rule (Article 356): Relationship and Implications
key_dimensions: Under Article 356, Council of Ministers is either dismissed or suspended — President's Rule imposed
Governor's report to President: CM cannot prevent Governor's report — key constitutional check
S.R. Bommai vs. Union of India (1994): Floor test mandatory before recommending President's Rule; Assembly should not be dissolved before Presidential approval
UPSC trap: During President's Rule, Governor acts as agent of President — CM and Council cease to function

concepts.name: States Without Legislative Council: Impact on CM and Ministerial Composition
key_dimensions: Only 6 states have Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad) — Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh
In states without LC, a non-MLA appointed as minister MUST get elected to Legislative Assembly within 6 months — no alternative upper house route
Contrast: At Union level, a non-Lok Sabha member appointed minister can be/become a Rajya Sabha member
UPSC trap: This asymmetry means the minister-from-upper-house route is only available in 6 states — critical factual distinction

concepts.name: Sarkaria and Punchhi Commission Recommendations on CM-Governor-Centre Relations
key_dimensions: Sarkaria Commission (1988): Governor should be an eminent person, not actively involved in politics for last 5 years; CM must be consulted in appointment of Governor
Punchhi Commission (2010): Governor should not be immune from legal proceedings after retirement; 'localisation' of Governor appointment
Both commissions recommended Governor should not delay giving assent to State Bills
UPSC relevance: Recommendations frequently cited in answer writing on Centre-State relations and federal tensions
